drapeaux.note: Imperial decree of April 24, 1863 (Le Moniteur universel). No official English text was retrieved. The English wording is a span of the translation published in English Wikipedia, "Salon des Refusés" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon_des_Refus%C3%A9s: "wishing to let the public judge the legitimacy of these complaints"), copied word for word and checked against the French text of the decree as quoted in French Wikipedia ("voulant laisser le public juge de la légitimité de ces réclamations"). "Réclamations" is therefore rendered "complaints" (also in the quiz).

Manet's nickname "la partie carrée" is kept in French with the gloss "the foursome". The French phrase was seen in French Wikipedia ("Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe") and on histoire-image.org, which both report that Manet called the painting this; the Musée d'Orsay notice cited by the entry could not be read (403), so the source itself is unverified.

accroche: The official jury rejects his painting. The same year, the emperor himself orders the exhibition that will make him famous.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the spring of 1863, the jury of the official Paris Salon, the exhibition that makes or breaks a painter's career under the Second Empire, rejects more than 3,000 of the 5,000 works submitted to it. Among those turned down: Camille Pissarro, Johan Jongkind, Henri Harpignies, Henri Fantin-Latour, James Whistler, and a certain Édouard Manet, with a canvas he titled *Le Bain* (The Bath).

The excluded artists vigorously protest the verdict. Informed of the dispute, Emperor Napoleon III, who considered the jury too harsh, decides that an exhibition of the rejected works will be held at the Palais de l'Industrie, where the public can see the discarded works for themselves. It opens on May 15, 1863, alongside the official Salon, with 1,200 works in twelve rooms; a committee of rejected artists compiles the catalogue, and 871 artists take part, many of the rejected having withdrawn their canvases rather than show them there. This is the Salon des Refusés (Salon of the Rejected).

## The Scandal

Manet's canvas, since renamed *Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe* (The Luncheon on the Grass), provokes a scandal that is as much aesthetic as moral, and harsh criticism. Yet it draws on a perfectly respectable heritage: the composition of the central group derives from an engraving by Marcantonio Raimondi after Raphael, *The Judgment of Paris*, and the general subject owes something to the *Concert champêtre* (Pastoral Concert), a painting then attributed to Giorgione and held in the Louvre.

Manet subverts these models. A nude woman, looking at the viewer, sits among men dressed as contemporaries, with none of the mythological or allegorical pretext that tradition required to justify nudity. Manet himself familiarly calls his canvas "la Partie carrée" (the foursome). The execution shocks as much as the subject: the sketchy landscape looks like a stage set, the laws of perspective are broken (the woman in the background should be smaller), and gradations are abandoned in favor of contrasts of light and color.

## What It Shifts

The Salon des Refusés was not designed to rehabilitate anyone. The imperial decree, published in *Le Moniteur universel* on April 24, 1863, goes no further than an administrative measure: "to let the public be the judge of the legitimacy" of the rejected artists' complaints, without taking sides for or against the jury. The effect goes far beyond this modest gesture. The exhibition brings together in one place artists of modernity and allows some of them to become famous, like Manet, whose painting sets off one of the most violent controversies in nineteenth-century art history.

The exhibition is not repeated in the following years. It takes until 1884 and the Salon des Indépendants, whose motto is "without jury or awards," for all artists to be able to show their work freely. According to Wikipedia, the Salon des Refusés marks the beginning of the end of the Academy and of the Salon as the single institution for distributing works of art. *Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe*, mocked in 1863, is now on display at the Musée d'Orsay in Paris.

repere.texte: Manet's painting, rejected and shown in 1863 under the title Le Bain, was also familiarly called "la Partie carrée" by him before becoming known as Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe.

carte.punch: The jury rejects his painting. The same year, the emperor orders the exhibition that makes him famous.
carte.idee: In 1863, the jury of the official Paris Salon rejects more than 3,000 of the 5,000 works submitted, including Manet's. Napoleon III orders a parallel exhibition, the Salon des Refusés. Manet's painting, a nude woman among clothed men, becomes the scandal of the year.

quiz.question: Why does Napoleon III order the opening of the Salon des Refusés in 1863?
choix: To offer an official platform to the artists he personally considered the most talented
In the face of the scale of the protests by artists rejected en masse by the official Salon jury that year
Because the official Salon had accidentally destroyed some of the submitted works
At the request of the Louvre museum, which wanted to exhibit copies of classical works
quiz.explication: It is the rejection of more than 3,000 of the 5,000 works submitted to the 1863 official Salon jury, and the scale of the protests that followed, that lead Napoleon III, who found the jury too harsh, to order a parallel exhibition where the public can judge the discarded canvases for itself. The decree speaks only of "complaints": no judgment on the artists' talent, no accident, and no request from the Louvre is involved.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which earlier works does Manet borrow from to compose Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe?
choix: A fresco by Michelangelo and a drawing by Leonardo da Vinci held in the Vatican
An engraving by Marcantonio Raimondi after Raphael, and the Concert champêtre attributed to Giorgione
A painting by Rembrandt and an ancient Greek sculpture displayed at the British Museum
A watercolor by Delacroix and a Japanese print by Hokusai held in Tokyo
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The composition of the central group derives from an engraving by Raimondi after Raphael, The Judgment of Paris, and the subject owes something to the Pastoral Concert, then attributed to Giorgione and held in the Louvre.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does the imperial decree published in Le Moniteur universel on April 24, 1863, say?
choix: That the public should be left to judge the legitimacy of the rejected artists' complaints
That the official Salon jury acted unjustly and must be dissolved
That the rejected artists will receive financial compensation from the state
That the Salon des Refusés will permanently replace the official Salon
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The decree goes no further than a measure of order, leaving the public to judge the legitimacy of the complaints, without taking sides for or against the jury.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What in Manet's painting technique shocks the public as much as the subject of the painting?
choix: The use of fluorescent colors unusual for the period
A canvas far larger than the dimensions allowed at the Salon
Giving up gradations in favor of contrasts of light and color, and breaking the laws of perspective
The total absence of human figures in the composition
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Manet abandons gradations in favor of contrasts of light and color, and breaks the laws of perspective: the woman in the background should be smaller.
